title: Tobin and the Grammar Gremlin
markdown:
The Great Burrow Academy buzzed like a happy bumblebee convention. Banner-making day: cheerful colours, the scratch of stitching. For Tobin the mole it felt more like a stampede of nervous grasshoppers. Whiskers twitching, tummy flip-flopping, he scuttled toward the main hall. There hung the Burrow Badgers’ football banner, letters wobbling more than jelly on a trampoline: WE’S THE BEST!

His mole heart tumbled. “We’s?” The apostrophe sat there like a smug crumb. He spent afternoons in the library on punctuation’s funny quirks. He dreamed of grammar-club champion. How, when the school was shouting this at the forest? The old urge arrived: burrow down, down, until the disaster was a rumour told by someone else. A dewdrop-sized spark said no, and sparks, even small ones, are stubborn.

He straightened his spectacles, counted to three because one was not enough courage, and marched to Mrs. Sniffleton, a kind badger whose glasses always looked ready to slide. Paint pots clattered. Someone sang off-key on purpose. “Excuse me. The banner is splendid. There might be a grammar mistake.”

She beamed, spectacles halfway down, perpetually surprised. “Mistake? We’s the Best! Spirit. Enthusiasm.”

“The correct way is We are the best. Or We’re, with an apostrophe for missing letters. We’s sounds like something that belongs to us. The badger’s favourite turnip.” He wiggled his nose to show the difference between belonging and being.

She peered, furrowed, tapped a claw. “We are the best hasn’t the same zing. We’s has oomph.” A pat on the head that meant run along. “Finished. Perfectly lovely.”

Tobin’s hope hissed out. He dragged away. The colours dulled.

A deep rumbly voice cut the clatter. “A sharp ear for correct words?”

Captain Reed, owl of the tallest oak, sat on a tall stool: on time, precise, no patience for mess in nests or sentences. Tobin explained. The owl listened until Tobin felt heard. “A serious error. We’s is a mess. Every mistake can be fixed with cleverness and a little nerve. We put our heads together.”

The idea was simple: a corrected slogan beside the original, not a midnight raid on the finished banner, which would have been a different sort of mess. Tobin fetched clean fabric from the craft cupboard — the piece without jam stains — and his neatest paints. He ruled faint guidelines, then painted WE ARE THE BEST! in letters that did not wobble even when his paws wanted to. He held it up, a small shining example. Captain Reed inspected the apostrophe situation and, finding none required, looked almost pleased.

Then a flash of red fur. Nell the fox, eyes on a dazzling butterfly that had come in the window, tumbled headfirst into the wet banner and knocked the pot of permanent blue ink Mrs. Sniffleton insisted on for official work. Sploosh. Tobin’s careful letters became a swirl. Nell yelped, warrior-smear on her cheek. “Sorry! The butterfly was impossibly shiny.”

Tobin stared. Whiskers trembled. The end, he thought, and did not name the feeling as if naming it would help.

Captain Reed cleared his throat, low. “Temporary. Not a disaster. Nell has, in her way, made something artistic. And you — the ink-cleaning trick. Grandmother. Stubborn berry stains.”

Rainwater from leaves, finely ground chalk. A long shot. Their only one.

They worked in a side corridor that smelled of boots and determination. Nell, suddenly good with a rag, spread the paste in careful circles instead of her usual dashes. Tobin, precise claws, lifted the stubborn blue as if each letter were a shy insect. Earthy chalk smell, swish of cloth, a race against the bell that would call everyone to the hall. The butterfly, unhelpful, sat on a windowsill and cleaned its wings. Bit by bit the harsh colour faded. A smear tried to become a new word and was politely discouraged. WE ARE THE BEST! remained, lighter, like a memory that had decided to stay. Nell’s cheek still wore blue. She left it. “Evidence,” she said, “that I have met ink and survived.”

At the unveiling Mrs. Sniffleton presented the original, beaming as if oomph were a curriculum. The crowd murmured. WE’S THE BEST! still glared, spirit intact, grammar not. A hedgehog in the second row mouthed we’s as if tasting it and made a face. Then Nell and Tobin, ink-stained and beaming, held up the second banner, faded in places, clear: WE ARE THE BEST! Captain Reed, from the rafters, did not hoot a speech. He blinked once, which in owl is a paragraph.

Silence, then applause that had been waiting. They cheered the mole who had spoken, the fox who had cleaned what she had spilled, the owl who only nodded, a sparkle doing the rest.

From that day the Academy banner read, in letters that knew their job, WE ARE THE BEST! Mrs. Sniffleton, after a long look and a longer silence, had the original taken down “for archival spirit” and the corrected one hung where oomph could still be heard if you knew the story. Tobin felt a warmth better than any deep tunnel. He logged we’s / chalk paste / two banners in the library book, left a spare apostrophe in his pencil tin in case of emergencies, and let Nell keep a blue smudge as a souvenir she had earned. Captain Reed flew back to the oak on time, which was his idea of a party. Grammar-club champion, in the quiet way, had arrived wearing spectacles and a bit of chalk.
